recommended_action: Consider dengue fever as a probable diagnosis when the clinical presentation is compatible; do not treat this card alone as diagnostic confirmation.
exclusions_or_missing_information: Laboratory confirmation and differential diagnosis may still be required depending on the case.

source.title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue

evidence: Classical dengue fever is characterized by high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia and rashes; leucopenia and thrombocytopenia are usually observed.

recommended_action: Identify dengue warning signs and consider escalation or closer clinical assessment when present.
conditions: intense continuous abdominal pain
persistent vomiting
fluid accumulation
mucosal bleeding
altered mental status
hepatomegaly
progressive increase of haematocrit
exclusions_or_missing_information: If warning-sign status is unknown, the system should not assume absence.

source.title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue

evidence: Warning signs include intense continuous abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, altered mental status, hepatomegaly, and progressive increase of haematocrit.

recommended_action: At the first visit, perform CBC and dengue NS1 antigen or anti-dengue antibody testing according to the day of illness. If the patient presents within 5 days of fever, obtain baseline CBC, haematocrit, NS1 antigen, SGOT and SGPT.
conditions: test selection depends on day of illness
exclusions_or_missing_information: day of illness should be known to select the most appropriate dengue diagnostic test

source.title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue

evidence: CBC and NS-1 Ag/Anti-Dengue Ab should be done in suspected dengue patients at first visit depending on day of presentation; within 5 days CBC, haematocrit, NS1 antigen, SGOT and SGPT are recommended for baseline assessment.

recommended_action: Provide home-based care with adequate rest, oral hydration, urine-output monitoring, fever control with paracetamol, education about warning signs, and daily follow-up as appropriate.
conditions: home management is intended for patients without warning signs, coexisting conditions, or social risk

medication.name: Paracetamol
medication.dose: Do not exceed 3 g/day in adults; 60 mg/kg/24 hours in children
medication.frequency: as clinically required within maximum daily dose
medication.instructions: Do not take excess paracetamol even if fever does not fully settle.

advice: Use oral fluids with electrolytes rather than plain water alone
Encourage urination every 3-4 hours and monitor urine output
Avoid NSAIDs including COX-2 inhibitors and steroids
Return immediately if clinical deterioration or warning features appear
exclusions_or_missing_information: body weight where weight-based fluid advice is needed

source.title: National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue

evidence: Home management includes rest, paracetamol with a maximum of 3 g/day in adults or 60 mg/kg/24 hours in children, adequate oral hydration, urine monitoring, warning-sign education, avoidance of NSAIDs and steroids, and follow-up with return for hospitalization if deterioration occurs.

recommended_action: Confirm hypertension using repeated blood pressure measurements rather than a single office reading. In general, use at least three BP measurements per visit across two to three visits at 1-4 week intervals. A diagnosis may be made at a single visit if BP is at least 160/100 mmHg or there is evidence of hypertension-mediated organ damage.
conditions: single-visit diagnosis may be appropriate when BP is at least 160/100 mmHg or HMOD is present
evidence: Hypertension diagnosis should be based on multiple blood pressure measurements on separate occasions; generally at least three measurements per visit and two to three visits at 1-4 week intervals, with possible single-visit diagnosis at BP >=160/100 mmHg or with hypertension-mediated organ damage.

recommended_action: Perform baseline investigations for hypertension including serum sodium, potassium, creatinine with eGFR, urine dipstick, and 12-lead ECG. If available, obtain lipid profile and fasting glucose. Additional investigations should depend on suspicion of secondary hypertension or hypertension-mediated organ damage.
conditions: testing should not unnecessarily delay treatment when treatment is clinically indicated
exclusions_or_missing_information: possible secondary cause or organ damage
evidence: All hypertensive patients should undergo a limited number of investigations including sodium, potassium, serum creatinine and eGFR, urine dipstick, and 12-lead ECG; lipid profile and fasting glucose may be obtained if available.

symptoms_or_prerequisites: adult with hypertension requiring pharmacological treatment
recommended_action: Use the national primary-care stepwise antihypertensive protocol: start amlodipine 5 mg once daily; if target blood pressure is not reached after review, add losartan 50 mg once daily; if still uncontrolled, add hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg once daily and consider referral when appropriate.
conditions: review response after treatment initiation or change
treatment choice must consider patient-specific contraindications and comorbidities

medication.name: Losartan
medication.instructions: add if blood pressure remains above target

medication.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
medication.instructions: add if blood pressure remains above target despite prior steps

evidence: The national primary-care hypertension management protocol presents stepwise treatment beginning with amlodipine 5 mg once daily, followed by addition of losartan 50 mg once daily and then hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg once daily when target blood pressure is not achieved.

recommended_action: Review monthly after starting or changing antihypertensive treatment until target blood pressure is reached; once controlled, follow up every 3-6 months. Refer to an appropriate specialist when accelerated or malignant hypertension, suspected secondary hypertension, resistant hypertension, recent target-organ damage, pregnancy, or age under 18 years is present.
conditions: follow-up interval depends on blood pressure control and treatment changes
advice: monthly review until target BP is achieved
refer when specialist indications are present
evidence: Monthly follow-up is recommended after initiation or change in antihypertensive medication until target BP is reached; once target is achieved, follow-up every 3-6 months is appropriate. Referral is indicated for accelerated or malignant hypertension, suspected secondary hypertension, resistant hypertension, recent target-organ damage, pregnancy, and children under 18 years.

recommended_action: Consider suspected cholera according to outbreak context. Outside a declared cholera outbreak, a patient aged 2 years or older with acute watery diarrhoea and severe dehydration, or dying from acute watery diarrhoea, meets the suspected cholera case definition. During a declared cholera outbreak, any person presenting with or dying from acute watery diarrhoea meets the suspected case definition.
conditions: case definition depends on whether a cholera outbreak has been declared
outside an outbreak, age and severe dehydration status are required
exclusions_or_missing_information: presence or absence of severe dehydration

source.title: Clinical tools for cholera treatment facilities

evidence: Outside a cholera outbreak, suspected cholera includes a patient aged at least 2 years with acute watery diarrhoea and severe dehydration or dying from acute watery diarrhoea; during a declared outbreak, any person presenting with or dying from acute watery diarrhoea meets the suspected case definition.

symptoms_or_prerequisites: suspected cholera or acute watery diarrhoea
recommended_action: Classify dehydration severity before selecting treatment. Severe dehydration is present with one or more danger signs such as lethargy or unconsciousness, absent or weak pulse, or respiratory distress, or with at least two severe dehydration findings such as sunken eyes, inability to drink or drinking poorly, and a skin pinch that returns very slowly. Some dehydration is considered when there are no danger signs and at least two findings such as irritability or restlessness, sunken eyes, rapid pulse, thirst with eager drinking, or a skin pinch that returns slowly. If the patient is awake and alert with normal pulse, normal thirst, eyes not sunken and normal skin pinch, classify as no dehydration.
conditions: dehydration classification determines Plan A, Plan B, or Plan C

source.title: Clinical tools for cholera treatment facilities

evidence: Severe dehydration requires Plan C, some dehydration requires Plan B, and no dehydration requires Plan A, based on danger signs and dehydration findings.

recommended_action: For severe dehydration, start intravenous Ringer's lactate immediately. For infants under 12 months, give 30 mL/kg in 1 hour followed by 70 mL/kg over the next 5 hours. For patients aged 12 months or older, give 30 mL/kg in 30 minutes followed by 70 mL/kg over the next 2.5 hours. Reassess at least every 15-30 minutes and give ORS to replace ongoing losses as soon as the patient can drink safely.
conditions: use Plan C only when severe dehydration or shock criteria are met
age is required to determine infusion timing

medication.name: Ringer's lactate
medication.instructions: under 12 months: 30 mL/kg in 1 hour then 70 mL/kg over 5 hours; 12 months or older: 30 mL/kg in 30 minutes then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 hours

source.title: Clinical tools for cholera treatment facilities

evidence: For severe dehydration, intravenous fluids should be started immediately with Ringer's lactate as first choice. Give 30 mL/kg followed by 70 mL/kg, with timing based on age, reassess every 15-30 minutes, and give ORS for ongoing losses when the patient can drink safely.

recommended_action: For some dehydration, use Plan B with oral rehydration solution over 4 hours and reassess at least every hour. Give additional ORS to replace ongoing stool losses.
conditions: Plan B applies when there are no danger signs and the patient meets criteria for some dehydration
ORS volume depends on age and weight

medication.name: Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)
medication.frequency: over 4 hours plus additional ORS for ongoing losses
medication.instructions: <4 months and <5 kg: 200-400 mL; 4-11 months and 5-8 kg: 400-600 mL; 12-23 months and 8-12 kg: 600-800 mL; 2-4 years and 12-16 kg: 800-1200 mL; 4-14 years and 16-30 kg: 1200-2200 mL; 15 years or older and 30 kg or more: 2200-4000 mL

source.title: Clinical tools for cholera treatment facilities

evidence: For some dehydration, give ORS over 4 hours according to age and weight, reassess at least every hour, and give additional ORS to replace ongoing losses.

recommended_action: For patients with no signs of dehydration, use Plan A. Give ORS after each loose stool according to age and continue oral hydration. For patients under 24 months give 50-100 mL after each loose stool; for ages 2-9 years give 100-200 mL; for patients aged 10 years or older give as much as wanted.
conditions: Plan A applies only when no dehydration is present
ORS amount depends on age

medication.name: Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)
medication.instructions: <24 months: 50-100 mL; 2-9 years: 100-200 mL; 10 years or older: as much as wanted

medication.name: Zinc
medication.dose: 10 mg if under 6 months; 20 mg if over 6 months
medication.instructions: pediatric recommendation from the WHO tool

source.title: Clinical tools for cholera treatment facilities

evidence: For no dehydration, Plan A recommends ORS after each loose stool according to age. Zinc is given for 10 days in children, with 10 mg once daily under 6 months and 20 mg once daily over 6 months.

recommended_action: Use antibiotics when the patient has severe dehydration, is pregnant, or is elderly. Preferred treatment is single-dose doxycycline; azithromycin is an alternative. Do not recommend antibiotics solely from this card if these applicability criteria are unknown.
conditions: antibiotics are indicated for severe dehydration, pregnancy, or elderly patients
drug and dose selection depends on age

medication.name: Doxycycline
medication.dose: 200 mg if under 12 years; 300 mg for older children and adults

medication.name: Azithromycin
medication.dose: 20 mg/kg if under 12 years; 1 g for older children and adults

source.title: Clinical tools for cholera treatment facilities

evidence: Antibiotics are recommended for all patients with severe dehydration, pregnant women, and elderly patients. Doxycycline is preferred as a single dose; azithromycin is an alternative single-dose regimen.

recommended_action: Consider chikungunya when there is sudden onset of fever with joint manifestations and rash. A possible case meets clinical criteria; a probable case meets both clinical and epidemiological criteria; a confirmed case requires laboratory criteria.
conditions: clinical criteria include fever above 38.5 C and severe arthralgia or arthritis not explained by another condition
epidemiological criteria include residence in or travel to an epidemic area or reported transmission within 15 days before symptom onset
exclusions_or_missing_information: recent travel or residence in epidemic area

source.title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever

evidence: Chikungunya should be suspected with sudden onset fever, joint manifestations and rash. Possible cases meet clinical criteria, probable cases meet both clinical and epidemiological criteria, and confirmed cases meet laboratory criteria.

recommended_action: Select chikungunya testing according to the day of illness. Use real-time RT-PCR within 5 days of symptom onset. Viral-specific IgM can be tested from 5 to 28 days after fever onset. A four-fold rise in IgG can be assessed using samples collected at least three weeks apart, with the first sample after day 7. Routine investigations may include CBC, C-reactive protein and SGPT.
conditions: test choice depends on day of illness
RT-PCR availability may be limited

source.title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever

evidence: Specific laboratory investigations include RT-PCR within 5 days of illness, IgM in a serum sample collected 5-28 days after fever onset, and four-fold rise of IgG in paired samples. Routine investigations include CBC, CRP and SGPT.

recommended_action: Manage mild or moderate chikungunya supportively at home with adequate fluids containing electrolytes, rest, and paracetamol for fever when appropriate. Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs during the acute phase, and do not use NSAIDs unless dengue has been adequately excluded.
conditions: home management is appropriate for mild or moderate cases
severe cases require hospital management
paracetamol dosing must consider liver or kidney disease
NSAIDs should not be used until dengue is excluded

medication.name: Paracetamol
medication.dose: up to 1000 mg per dose in adults
medication.frequency: up to four times daily during fever
medication.instructions: use only in persons without pre-existing liver or kidney disease; children may receive 50-60 mg/kg/day in divided doses

advice: consume plenty of water with electrolytes
avoid self-medication with aspirin or NSAIDs
avoid heat over painful joints in the acute stage
mild exercise or physiotherapy during recovery

source.title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever

evidence: Mild and moderate cases can be managed at home with fluids, paracetamol and rest. Aspirin and NSAIDs should be avoided in the acute stage, and NSAIDs should be used only when dengue has been adequately excluded.
